articles.title: These Are the 10 Most Dangerous Toys of the Year, According to Safety Experts
articles.content:
Halloween is over, and the next big kids’ holiday is right around the corner. No, not Thanksgiving! (What kid has ever handed you a wish list for turkey?) Of course, I am talking about the December gift-giving holidays, including Christmas. If your kid hasn’t started pestering you about that absolutely-must-have toy yet, you know it’s coming.
But all toys are not created equal, and with the commotion of the season, it’s easy to miss some major red flags when it comes to safety. Enter an organization called World Against Toys Causing Harm (aka W.A.T.C.H.). For more than 50 years, W.A.T.C.H. has put out an annual 10 Worst Toys list to help parents and other gift givers stay vigilant when buying toys.
According to the Consumer Product Safety Commission (CSPC), hospital emergency rooms saw nearly 270,000 toy-related injuries in 2025, and 68% of them involved kids under 14. That works out to one every two minutes! Nearly half of those ER visits (45%) involved injuries to the head or face, by far the most commonly injured area.
Ahead, we’ll take you through W.A.T.C.H.’s 10 Worst Toys report for 2026, explain how they came up with the list and give you some smart holiday gift-buying tips. Read on for all the details, and stay safe out there.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more news, holidays, humor, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
W.A.T.C.H. does not publish its methodology for choosing the most dangerous toys of the year, but the director of the nonprofit organization, consumer advocate James A. Swartz, has explained the approach in the past.
“We shop for toys, the same way parents and caregivers do, to survey the marketplace,” Swartz told Fast Company in 2019. “The 10 Worst List provides examples of types of hazards acknowledged by the industry over decades—small parts, choking hazards and other examples of hazards as represented by the nominees on the list.”
The group is not a testing organization, and stresses that its goal is to educate parents and the public on hazards posed by toys. The top 10 “worst” toys are intended to be representative of the hazards commonly found in the market, not serve as an exhaustive list.
This is the 54th year that W.A.T.C.H. has released its list of the most dangerous toys, and this year’s roster is filled with familiar hazards, including suffocation, blunt force trauma and eye injuries. Here are the top 10 toys to skip this year and why, according to W.A.T.C.H.
W.A.T.C.H. is focused on educating consumers about potential harms caused by toys, so the products it calls out on this annual list are not necessarily involved in a recall. But that’s why the group does this reporting, according to W.A.T.C.H. president Joan E. Siff, who is also a board member at Boston’s Franciscan Children’s Hospital.
“A recall should not be the first line of defense against a dangerous toy,” Siff said in this year’s W.A.T.C.H. press release. “Some unsafe products are never recalled, and recalled toys may remain in homes and classrooms long after a warning is issued.”
W.A.T.C.H. points out that since last year’s report, 77 products—more than 1.6 million individual toys—have been recalled due to safety concerns. According to the organization, this stat points to why parents should not wait for a recall to take action. Just a few years ago, a toy on W.A.T.C.H.’s list was implicated in the deaths of two toddlers and was subsequently recalled.
Since the beginning of the school year, 18 toys have been recalled, according to the search tool at the CSPC. Here are the most recent highlights, followed by the reason for the recall.
Christmas doesn’t have to be a fraught experience, but with the craziness of the holidays, it’s easy to lose track of what your kids are doing after they rip open their presents. Buying smart and keeping up on the latest guidance can help all year round. Here’s what to do.

articles.summary:
Halloween is over, and the next big kids’ holiday is right around the corner. No, not Thanksgiving! (What kid has ever handed you a wish list for turkey?) Of course, I am talking about the December gift-giving holidays, including Christmas. If your kid hasn’t started pestering you about that absolutely-must-have toy yet, you know it’s coming.

But all toys are not created equal, and with the commotion of the season, it’s easy to miss some major red flags when it comes to safety. Enter an organization called World Against Toys Causing Harm (aka W.A.T.C.H.). For more than 50 years, W.A.T.C.H. has put out an annual 10 Worst Toys list to help parents and other gift givers stay vigilant when buying toys.

According to the Consumer Product Safety Commission (CSPC), hospital emergency rooms saw nearly 270,000 toy-related injuries in 2025, and 68% of them involved kids under 14. That works out to one every two minutes! Nearly half of those ER visits (45%) involved injuries to the head or face, by far the most commonly injured area.

Ahead, we’ll take you through W.A.T.C.H.’s 10 Worst Toys report for 2026, explain how they came up with the list and give you some smart holiday gift-buying tips. Read on for all the details, and stay safe out there.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more news, holidays, humor, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.

How did the report determine the most dangerous toys of the year?

W.A.T.C.H. does not publish its methodology for choosing the most dangerous toys of the year, but the director of the nonprofit organization, consumer advocate James A. Swartz, has explained the approach in the past.

“We shop for toys, the same way parents and caregivers do, to survey the marketplace,” Swartz told Fast Company in 2019. “The 10 Worst List provides examples of types of hazards acknowledged by the industry over decades—small parts, choking hazards and other examples of hazards as represented by the nominees on the list.”

The group is not a testing organization, and stresses that its goal is to educate parents and the public on hazards posed by toys. The top 10 “worst” toys are intended to be representative of the hazards commonly found in the market, not serve as an exhaustive list.

What are the most dangerous toys of 2026?

This is the 54th year that W.A.T.C.H. has released its list of the most dangerous toys, and this year’s roster is filled with familiar hazards, including suffocation, blunt force trauma and eye injuries. Here are the top 10 toys to skip this year and why, according to W.A.T.C.H.

  • PBJ’s Plush Ball Jellies Rainbow Unicorn: Choking and ingestion risk for children 5 years old and under
  • Snackles Sulley (pictured above): Suffocation risk for infants
  • Zuru XShot Performance Break Barrel Dart Blaster: Risk of eye injuries for all users
  • Marvel’s The Thing Clobberin’ FX Fists: Risk of blunt force and impact injuries for all users
  • Wilberry Owl: Aspiration and ingestion risk for young children
  • Faux Bow Protégé: Eye and face injury risk for all users
  • Our Generation Hop In Cat Carrier: Choking hazard for young children
  • Sky Rover KnightForce Helicopter: Risk of eye, face and other impact injuries for all users
  • Sweet Candy Perfume Lab: Risk of chemical-related injuries for all users
  • Original Koosh Slingshot: Eye-injury risk for all users

Why haven’t these toys been recalled?

W.A.T.C.H. is focused on educating consumers about potential harms caused by toys, so the products it calls out on this annual list are not necessarily involved in a recall. But that’s why the group does this reporting, according to W.A.T.C.H. president Joan E. Siff, who is also a board member at Boston’s Franciscan Children’s Hospital.

“A recall should not be the first line of defense against a dangerous toy,” Siff said in this year’s W.A.T.C.H. press release. “Some unsafe products are never recalled, and recalled toys may remain in homes and classrooms long after a warning is issued.”

W.A.T.C.H. points out that since last year’s report, 77 products—more than 1.6 million individual toys—have been recalled due to safety concerns. According to the organization, this stat points to why parents should not wait for a recall to take action. Just a few years ago, a toy on W.A.T.C.H.’s list was implicated in the deaths of two toddlers and was subsequently recalled.

Which toys have been recalled recently?

Since the beginning of the school year, 18 toys have been recalled, according to the search tool at the CSPC. Here are the most recent highlights, followed by the reason for the recall.

  • Kakgold 4WD Stunt Vehicle Toys (pictured above): Button cell and lithium-ion batteries pose a deadly ingestion hazard.
  • Magnetopia Magnetic Building Cubes and Blocks: Magnets within the toys can attract each other when swallowed, causing severe damage to body tissues.
  • Arlopu Slide Playsets: Holes in the slide panels can trap a child’s head.
  • Shein Spiral Toys: These toys have small parts that detach, posing a choking hazard.
  • Avengers Infinity Gauntlet Medals: Another magnet-involved recall involving an ingestion hazard.

What safety tips should you keep in mind when buying toys for kids?

Christmas doesn’t have to be a fraught experience, but with the craziness of the holidays, it’s easy to lose track of what your kids are doing after they rip open their presents. Buying smart and keeping up on the latest guidance can help all year round. Here’s what to do.

  • Buy age-appropriate toys. Even if your child is advanced for their age, one moment of inattention can result in tragedy. By law, toys made for children under 3 cannot have small parts that could cause a choking hazard.
  • Read the fine print. Manufacturers have to disclose certain risks on the label, so read the label before buying.
  • Check the stitching. Stuffed animals and other toys with beads, buttons and stuffing should be well-made and sturdy enough to hold up to wear and tear.
  • Buy electronic toys that are UL approved. UL is an organization that certifies that toys and other products have been manufactured to specific safety standards.
  • Be careful with shooting toys. Gel blasters, fake guns and toys that shoot projectiles can cause eye injuries and be confused with real guns by law enforcement.

Sources:

  • W.A.T.C.H.: “W.A.T.C.H. Unveils Its 54th Annual ’10 Worst Toys’ Nominees for 2026”
  • CPSC: “Toy-Related Deaths and Injuries Calendar Year 2025”
  • Fast Company: “These 10 toys are supposedly the worst of 2019. Holiday shoppers, check this list twice”
  • CPSC: “Recalls & Product Safety Warnings”
  • CPSC: “Small Parts Ban and Choking Hazard Labeling”
  • HealthyChildren.org: “How to Buy Safe Toys: A Parent’s Guide”

articles.title: McDonald’s New Holiday Adult Happy Meal Has a Home Alone Twist—And a Surprising Side
articles.content: If you grew up in the ‘90s, chances are you’ve watched Home Alone more times than you can count. We must admit, Kevin McCallister’s hilarious family headcount mix-up and booby-trap shenanigans in the 1990 Christmas classic never seem to get old. McDonald’s is now bringing back some of that feel-good holiday nostalgia with a brand new menu item inspired by the beloved Christmas movie. There’s even a tasty surprise that Kevin himself would probably love. The new Home Alone Meal offers grown-ups their own take on the classic Happy Meal. Because why shouldn’t adults have a little fun sometimes too? The first thing you need to know is that this isn’t your typical Happy Meal. The limited-edition meal is available for breakfast, lunch or dinner and comes with your choice of a McDonald’s Sausage, Egg and Cheese McGriddle or a Big Mac, according to the company’s Nov. 17 announcement. Now here’s where things get fun. Remember Kevin’s famous cheese pizza order? The new Little Nero’s Pizza McShaker Fries, named after the fictional pizza parlor in the original Home Alone, come with a special seasoning made with tomato, garlic, Italian herbs and cheese. Just put the fries into the included McShaker bag, add the seasoning and give it a good shake. There’s even a new sauce to go with them. The Lovely Cheese Dipping Sauce combines tomato, Parmesan cheese, herbs and garlic for an extra taste of pizza. That’s not all. Each meal comes with one of four collectible pairs of Home Alone–themed socks featuring some of the film’s fan-favorite characters, scenes and memorable quotes. The meal is packaged in a beautiful cardboard box–shaped house that is sure to bring back memories of when you watched the film for the first time. For dessert, McDonald’s is also launching the Everything Sundae McFlurry in a sweet nod to Kevin’s room-service order in Home Alone 2. The treat combines vanilla soft-serve ice cream, hot fudge, Oreo cookie pieces and M&M’s. You’ll have to order this one separately, though. It isn’t included in the meal. McDonald’s just announced its limited-time holiday menu items, including the Home Alone Meal, and even enlisted Macaulay Culkin to help bring some holiday magic to its latest ad. 🎅🍟😊 https://t.co/AR3vyKxxBj — TMZ (@TMZ) November 17, 2026 Macaulay Culkin is getting in on the fun by reprising his role as Kevin in the new holiday campaign. “What I love about this collaboration is that the Home Alone Meal captures something bigger than just one character, it’s about the playful spirit that resonates with people across generations,” Culkin said in a release. “Bringing this to life with McDonald’s and getting to reexperience these moments with my own kids reminds me why fans keep coming back to Kevin’s story,” he added. “That’s the magic we’re celebrating here.” The Home Alone Meal arrives at participating McDonald’s nationwide on Tuesday, Dec. 1. It will be available for a limited time while supplies last. Add Reader’s Digest on Google! articles.summary:
If you grew up in the ‘90s, chances are you’ve watched Home Alone more times than you can count. We must admit, Kevin McCallister’s hilarious family headcount mix-up and booby-trap shenanigans in the 1990 Christmas classic never seem to get old.

McDonald’s is now bringing back some of that feel-good holiday nostalgia with a brand new menu item inspired by the beloved Christmas movie. There’s even a tasty surprise that Kevin himself would probably love.

The new Home Alone Meal offers grown-ups their own take on the classic Happy Meal. Because why shouldn’t adults have a little fun sometimes too?

What’s in McDonald’s new Home Alone meal?

The first thing you need to know is that this isn’t your typical Happy Meal. The limited-edition meal is available for breakfast, lunch or dinner and comes with your choice of a McDonald’s Sausage, Egg and Cheese McGriddle or a Big Mac, according to the company’s Nov. 17 announcement.

Now here’s where things get fun.

Remember Kevin’s famous cheese pizza order? The new Little Nero’s Pizza McShaker Fries, named after the fictional pizza parlor in the original Home Alone, come with a special seasoning made with tomato, garlic, Italian herbs and cheese. Just put the fries into the included McShaker bag, add the seasoning and give it a good shake. There’s even a new sauce to go with them. The Lovely Cheese Dipping Sauce combines tomato, Parmesan cheese, herbs and garlic for an extra taste of pizza.

That’s not all. Each meal comes with one of four collectible pairs of Home Alone–themed socks featuring some of the film’s fan-favorite characters, scenes and memorable quotes. The meal is packaged in a beautiful cardboard box–shaped house that is sure to bring back memories of when you watched the film for the first time.

For dessert, McDonald’s is also launching the Everything Sundae McFlurry in a sweet nod to Kevin’s room-service order in Home Alone 2. The treat combines vanilla soft-serve ice cream, hot fudge, Oreo cookie pieces and M&M’s. You’ll have to order this one separately, though. It isn’t included in the meal.

A familiar face is back to promote the new meal

McDonald’s just announced its limited-time holiday menu items, including the Home Alone Meal, and even enlisted Macaulay Culkin to help bring some holiday magic to its latest ad. 🎅🍟😊 https://t.co/AR3vyKxxBj

— TMZ (@TMZ) November 17, 2026

Macaulay Culkin is getting in on the fun by reprising his role as Kevin in the new holiday campaign.

“What I love about this collaboration is that the Home Alone Meal captures something bigger than just one character, it’s about the playful spirit that resonates with people across generations,” Culkin said in a release.

“Bringing this to life with McDonald’s and getting to reexperience these moments with my own kids reminds me why fans keep coming back to Kevin’s story,” he added. “That’s the magic we’re celebrating here.”

The Home Alone Meal arrives at participating McDonald’s nationwide on Tuesday, Dec. 1. It will be available for a limited time while supplies last.

articles.title: Here’s How to Answer 12 Awkward Holiday Questions from Nosy Friends and Family
articles.content:
The year my husband and I announced that we were expecting our second child, we did it at a holiday party at our house, handing out baby snowman ornaments. We were thrilled. One relative’s first response was to blurt, “Your first is only a year old! Was this an accident?!”
For the record, it wasn’t. Our first baby had taken us two years to conceive, so we assumed Baby No. 2 would take just as long. Surprise: It did not. (If I’ve learned one thing as a parent, it’s that children will always do whatever you least expect.) Also, for the record, our family planning was none of her business.
I wanted to say something snarky, like, “Oh, we just really enjoy the baby-making process. Do you need tips?” What I actually did was mumble, “Well, we’re really excited about this …” and move along, because I didn’t want to torch the celebratory mood.
If you’ve ever had a relative lob a conversational grenade between the appetizers and the pie, you know the feeling. You freeze. You stutter. And then the perfect comeback arrives at 2 a.m., fully formed and … completely useless.
Why do people ask questions like this? Emily Turinas, PhD, a licensed psychologist and communication expert, says, “Most of the time it’s a clumsy attempt to connect or show they care.” (I have decided to believe that about my relative. It is the holidays, after all.)
But we’ll leave the full psychology of nosy relatives for another day. Today’s job is giving you something to say. So I asked four experts for scripts: Turinas; Sandy Gerber, an emotional intelligence speaker, a communication trainer and the author of Emotional Magnetism; Igda Martinez, PsyD, a clinical psychologist based in New York who treats adults with social anxiety and hears about holiday gatherings in her office every year; and Danyail Lawton, a strategic communications professional who spent 23 years in the Air Force as an intelligence operations professional.
Memorize a few of their lines, and the next time someone asks about your love life, your paycheck or your waistline, you’ll be ready. Read on for the scripts you need before your next holiday get-together.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more holidays, family, humor, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
A prepared line lets you respond instead of react. Martinez explains that when you’re caught off guard, “your heart can speed up, your mind can go blank, and you may tend to overshare, freeze up or get defensive.” Sound familiar? That’s my mumble, in clinical terms. The fix, she says, is to decide what you want to say in advance: “You can decide ahead of time, from a calm state, what you’re comfortable sharing, rather than deciding under pressure.” This is also the strategy therapists use to deal with anxious patients: Rehearse the scary thing ahead of time to reduce the dread.
There’s research behind the rehearsal too. In a landmark analysis of 94 studies, researchers found that making a specific “if this happens, then I will do that” plan significantly boosted people’s follow-through on their goals and that these plans helped make the desired response more automatic. Those studies weren’t about holiday guilt trips, but the principle carries over: If Aunt Beryl asks about grandchildren, then I will say my line and ask about her garden.
Gerber calls her version of this SET, which stands for Stories, Experiences of interest and Trigger responses, and entails keeping a few short stories, fun topics and ready answers in your pocket. Being SET, she says, “makes you SET to engage and enjoy yourself.” She learned the habit from her dad, who used to debrief her mom in the car on the way to every holiday party about the hosts’ and guests’ jobs, kids, hobbies and news. “He walked in ready to engage, and he left loved for it,” she says.
If it helps, think of it as disaster preparedness for your social life. You hope you never need the flashlight and the canned beans, but you’ll be glad they’re in the closet when the lights go out. And just like a good emergency kit, it covers more than the one disaster you planned for. Even if nobody asks you these exact questions, you’ll be ready for something similar. As Gerber puts it, “When you prepare, you don’t have to think on the spot and can choose to gracefully end a conversation.”
These 12 are the greatest hits, based on what our experts hear about most. Pick the lines that sound like you, because a script you wouldn’t say out loud is a script you won’t use.
What to say: “I’m holding out for [insert celebrity of choice] to become available.” Or, if you prefer to skip the joke, try: “Nothing to report there, but I’ve really been into [this hobby] lately. Let me tell you about it.”
Why it works: Gerber says humor works because the person realizes they’ve overstepped, laughs and moves on. The hobby-based answer is brief, light and steers the conversation toward something you actually enjoy, which also gives the asker something to follow up on. “You don’t have to defend yourself,” Martinez says.
If the topic is a sore spot, Lawton recommends a gentler version of “none of your business,” such as: “Not to be rude, but I prefer not to talk about my personal life.” Opening with “Not to be rude,” Lawton says, helps the response land lighter.
One more thing worth knowing: In many Latino and immigrant families, Martinez says, questions like this can come from closeness, not judgment. She suggests answering with warmth and humor, as in: “I’m looking for someone as wonderful as you!” That honors the relationship and still keeps your boundary.
What to say: “When we have news, you’ll be one of the first to know!” Or, if you want to shut the door more firmly, try: “That’s a decision we’re making together, and there’s a lot that goes into it behind the scenes. We’ll share news when we’re ready.”
Why it works: Martinez says the “news” line speaks to what’s likely underneath the question, which is the asker’s desire to be included, and it closes the topic without a debate. “No one owes anyone else a timeline,” she says. The firmer version, which Turinas suggested, politely signals that this isn’t their business and that more is going on than they can see … without giving a single detail.
Gerber’s favorite move for this question is even shorter: “Why do you ask?” She says it works because it flips the question back to the asker and signals you’re not open to chatting about it. It’s also the line I wish I’d had in my back pocket for “Was this an accident?!” I still love my snarky fantasy version, but this response would have been more appropriate.
What to say: “I know you’d love that. It’s not something I’m getting into tonight, but how’s [your family, job, hobby]?” Or: “Wow, that’s a big topic for another time, but I will connect with you when there is news.”
Why it works: The first line names the wish behind the question, then sets the boundary. “When people feel heard, they often push less,” Martinez says. The second, explains Gerber, makes clear you won’t be discussing it while promising to circle back when there’s something to share.
If it’s your own parent asking, you may get this one on repeat, so keep your answer warm and identical every time. Turinas also reminds us why you never owe anyone a detailed answer: “These questions can be deeply painful for people facing infertility or loss, and you never owe anyone an explanation.”
What to say: “I miss you too. Let’s set up a time to meet. [Then give a time period that works for you.]”
Why it works: Guilt trips are often love in disguise. Martinez says this reply responds to the real issue behind the criticism and shifts to something concrete. If you don’t want to commit to a visit, you could try: “I wish I could more often. Life’s been full, but I’m really glad to be here now.”
Gerber adds a practical twist: Acknowledge what they’re feeling, explain briefly that work and commitments make your schedule tricky, and suggest a regular Zoom or FaceTime call to catch up. They’ll feel heard, and you’ll have a standing date instead of a standing guilt trip.
What to say: “Whoa, that’s a lot to unpack over turkey. I’d rather enjoy the party. Have you tried the stuffing? It’s amazing.” Or the no-frills option: “That’s between the two of us, and I’d rather not get into that tonight.”
Why it works: The first option, says Gerber, kindly calls out that this isn’t the time and place, setting your boundary and redirecting the conversation right away. The blunter line points out that you avoid badmouthing anyone and that you don’t want advice or mediation from the peanut gallery. Adding “tonight,” Martinez notes, softens the message without opening the door. Pro tip: Always have food or drink on hand (literally) to pivot to. The stuffing never judges.
What to say: “Thanks for asking. It’s a lot. I’d appreciate a break from thinking about it tonight. Tell me what you’ve been up to.”
Why it works: Many people who ask this one actually care, so Gerber’s answer is honest and reassures them while also making the topic off-limits for the evening. She thanks the other person for caring, states clearly that it’s not up for discussion and flips the conversation back to them. Either way, you don’t owe anyone a play-by-play of a hard time.
What to say: “The pay’s fair, and I enjoy the work. Want to know what I enjoy most?” Or, for the “real job” jab: “This is my real job, and I really enjoy it. Want to know what I enjoy most?” For a laugh, you can also try: “Enough that I was able to buy that [item you wanted]!”
Why it works: You’re answering the spirit of the question without getting caught up in numbers. “By inviting curiosity, you’re turning judgment into a conversation,” Martinez says, “and your calm confidence doesn’t give much with which to argue.”
If you’re between gigs or still figuring things out, Turinas also has a line for “So what are you doing with your life?” She suggests responding with: “Honestly, I’m figuring it out and enjoying the process.” It works, she says, because it “reframes uncertainty as a choice, not a failure.”
What to say: “Renting works for us right now. Have you seen the housing market?” Or: “Renting works for me. If anything breaks, I call the landlord; it’s their problem. Have you had anything break in your home recently?”
Why it works: Similar to the advice above about your career, the phrase “right now” frames renting as a choice, Martinez says, and pivots to a topic most people have opinions about.
The second version, says Gerber, is calm and confident and invites the asker to share their own homeowner woes. However, Gerber adds a warning about that one: There is always something to fix, so you may lose them to a 20-minute monologue about their gutters!
What to say: “I’m not going to talk about my body, but I’d love to hear how you’ve been.” Or, to keep it lighter at first: “I’m feeling good, thanks.” And if they push: “I’m not interested in talking about my body. How was your trip?”
Why it works: According to Turinas, this is one question that deserves a firm boundary rather than a joke. “Comments about weight can be genuinely harmful,” she says. Nobody has to justify, explain or defend their body—period.
If you’re feeling spicy, Gerber suggests turning the tables: “Before I answer that, you go first. Tell me something deeply personal about yourself.” She says the asker usually realizes the mistake and apologizes. Lawton has another zero-frills option: “That is a very disrespectful question, and I do not appreciate it.”
A note for readers from Martinez: Skip comments on anyone’s body this season, including compliments on weight loss. “You never know who’s dealing with illness, grief or an eating disorder.”
What to say: “Nope!” with a smile, and move on. If they persist: “If I have news like that, I’ll share when I’m ready.” Or, a lighter option: “No, just enjoying the holiday food.”
Why it works: A short, light answer ends the moment fast. And as Martinez points out, “You don’t have to rescue the asker from their embarrassment.” Gerber also likes the flip-back “Why do you ask?” here, delivered seriously, since it shows the person how personal the question really was.
Also, never ask this question yourself. As Martinez notes, the person in front of you could be in the middle of infertility treatments or coping with pregnancy loss.
What to say: “I just don’t, but I’d love a sparkling water!” Or, if you’d rather go with a laugh, Gerber suggests: “Trust me, if you’ve seen my dance moves, you know alcohol is unnecessary.”
Why it works: No reason is required, and people have many reasons to skip alcohol. Turinas says it plainly: “Giving reasons invites debate; a simple, upbeat answer ends it.” Martinez adds that keeping a drink in your hand, even a seltzer, cuts down on follow-ups.
For the minimalist, Lawton offers, “Not everyone drinks.”
What to say: “I’d love to keep tonight politics-free. Tell me about your trip!” Or: “I’m taking the night off from politics, but I want to hear about your trip.”
Why it works: This sets a boundary on the topic, not on the person, Martinez says. And if you do want to engage, Turinas says that’s fine too, as long as you stay calm and avoid aggression: “I see it differently, and here’s why.” Either way, you get to choose, and staying calm keeps it a conversation instead of a fight.
Here are a few more quick hits from Martinez because yes, there are a lot of holiday minefields.
Question: “Is that what you’re wearing?”
Response: “Yep, I feel great in it!”
Question: “Are you still in therapy?”
Response: “I am, and I highly recommend it!”
Question: “Why didn’t you bring [partner/the kids]?”
Response: “They send their love. It worked out better this way this year.”
Mostly this: Tone does the work, and shorter is better. Here’s how to deliver your lines like a pro.
Which brings me back to my mumbled “We’re really excited about this.” It wasn’t the comeback of the century, but it was kind, it kept the party going, and, eventually, it turned into the opening of an article. Win/win! Awkward moments really do make the best stories. Mine just took a while to find its punch line.
About the experts
At Reader’s Digest, we’re committed to producing high-quality content by writers with expertise and experience in their field in consultation with relevant, qualified experts. articles.summary:
The year my husband and I announced that we were expecting our second child, we did it at a holiday party at our house, handing out baby snowman ornaments. We were thrilled. One relative’s first response was to blurt, “Your first is only a year old! Was this an accident?!”

For the record, it wasn’t. Our first baby had taken us two years to conceive, so we assumed Baby No. 2 would take just as long. Surprise: It did not. (If I’ve learned one thing as a parent, it’s that children will always do whatever you least expect.) Also, for the record, our family planning was none of her business.

I wanted to say something snarky, like, “Oh, we just really enjoy the baby-making process. Do you need tips?” What I actually did was mumble, “Well, we’re really excited about this …” and move along, because I didn’t want to torch the celebratory mood.

If you’ve ever had a relative lob a conversational grenade between the appetizers and the pie, you know the feeling. You freeze. You stutter. And then the perfect comeback arrives at 2 a.m., fully formed and … completely useless.

Why do people ask questions like this? Emily Turinas, PhD, a licensed psychologist and communication expert, says, “Most of the time it’s a clumsy attempt to connect or show they care.” (I have decided to believe that about my relative. It is the holidays, after all.)

But we’ll leave the full psychology of nosy relatives for another day. Today’s job is giving you something to say. So I asked four experts for scripts: Turinas; Sandy Gerber, an emotional intelligence speaker, a communication trainer and the author of Emotional Magnetism; Igda Martinez, PsyD, a clinical psychologist based in New York who treats adults with social anxiety and hears about holiday gatherings in her office every year; and Danyail Lawton, a strategic communications professional who spent 23 years in the Air Force as an intelligence operations professional.

Memorize a few of their lines, and the next time someone asks about your love life, your paycheck or your waistline, you’ll be ready. Read on for the scripts you need before your next holiday get-together.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more holidays, family, humor, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.

Why does it help to have a prepared response to awkward questions?

A prepared line lets you respond instead of react. Martinez explains that when you’re caught off guard, “your heart can speed up, your mind can go blank, and you may tend to overshare, freeze up or get defensive.” Sound familiar? That’s my mumble, in clinical terms. The fix, she says, is to decide what you want to say in advance: “You can decide ahead of time, from a calm state, what you’re comfortable sharing, rather than deciding under pressure.” This is also the strategy therapists use to deal with anxious patients: Rehearse the scary thing ahead of time to reduce the dread.

There’s research behind the rehearsal too. In a landmark analysis of 94 studies, researchers found that making a specific “if this happens, then I will do that” plan significantly boosted people’s follow-through on their goals and that these plans helped make the desired response more automatic. Those studies weren’t about holiday guilt trips, but the principle carries over: If Aunt Beryl asks about grandchildren, then I will say my line and ask about her garden.

Gerber calls her version of this SET, which stands for Stories, Experiences of interest and Trigger responses, and entails keeping a few short stories, fun topics and ready answers in your pocket. Being SET, she says, “makes you SET to engage and enjoy yourself.” She learned the habit from her dad, who used to debrief her mom in the car on the way to every holiday party about the hosts’ and guests’ jobs, kids, hobbies and news. “He walked in ready to engage, and he left loved for it,” she says.

If it helps, think of it as disaster preparedness for your social life. You hope you never need the flashlight and the canned beans, but you’ll be glad they’re in the closet when the lights go out. And just like a good emergency kit, it covers more than the one disaster you planned for. Even if nobody asks you these exact questions, you’ll be ready for something similar. As Gerber puts it, “When you prepare, you don’t have to think on the spot and can choose to gracefully end a conversation.”

What awkward questions should you prepare for?

These 12 are the greatest hits, based on what our experts hear about most. Pick the lines that sound like you, because a script you wouldn’t say out loud is a script you won’t use.

“So are you seeing anyone?” or “Why are you still single?”

What to say: “I’m holding out for [insert celebrity of choice] to become available.” Or, if you prefer to skip the joke, try: “Nothing to report there, but I’ve really been into [this hobby] lately. Let me tell you about it.”

Why it works: Gerber says humor works because the person realizes they’ve overstepped, laughs and moves on. The hobby-based answer is brief, light and steers the conversation toward something you actually enjoy, which also gives the asker something to follow up on. “You don’t have to defend yourself,” Martinez says.

If the topic is a sore spot, Lawton recommends a gentler version of “none of your business,” such as: “Not to be rude, but I prefer not to talk about my personal life.” Opening with “Not to be rude,” Lawton says, helps the response land lighter. 

One more thing worth knowing: In many Latino and immigrant families, Martinez says, questions like this can come from closeness, not judgment. She suggests answering with warmth and humor, as in: “I’m looking for someone as wonderful as you!” That honors the relationship and still keeps your boundary.

“When are you two finally getting married?”

What to say: “When we have news, you’ll be one of the first to know!” Or, if you want to shut the door more firmly, try: “That’s a decision we’re making together, and there’s a lot that goes into it behind the scenes. We’ll share news when we’re ready.”

Why it works: Martinez says the “news” line speaks to what’s likely underneath the question, which is the asker’s desire to be included, and it closes the topic without a debate. “No one owes anyone else a timeline,” she says. The firmer version, which Turinas suggested, politely signals that this isn’t their business and that more is going on than they can see … without giving a single detail.

Gerber’s favorite move for this question is even shorter: “Why do you ask?” She says it works because it flips the question back to the asker and signals you’re not open to chatting about it. It’s also the line I wish I’d had in my back pocket for “Was this an accident?!” I still love my snarky fantasy version, but this response would have been more appropriate.

“When are you going to give your parents some grandchildren?”

What to say: “I know you’d love that. It’s not something I’m getting into tonight, but how’s [your family, job, hobby]?” Or: “Wow, that’s a big topic for another time, but I will connect with you when there is news.”

Why it works: The first line names the wish behind the question, then sets the boundary. “When people feel heard, they often push less,” Martinez says. The second, explains Gerber, makes clear you won’t be discussing it while promising to circle back when there’s something to share.

If it’s your own parent asking, you may get this one on repeat, so keep your answer warm and identical every time. Turinas also reminds us why you never owe anyone a detailed answer: “These questions can be deeply painful for people facing infertility or loss, and you never owe anyone an explanation.”

“Why don’t you come home more often?”

What to say: “I miss you too. Let’s set up a time to meet. [Then give a time period that works for you.]”

Why it works: Guilt trips are often love in disguise. Martinez says this reply responds to the real issue behind the criticism and shifts to something concrete. If you don’t want to commit to a visit, you could try: “I wish I could more often. Life’s been full, but I’m really glad to be here now.”

Gerber adds a practical twist: Acknowledge what they’re feeling, explain briefly that work and commitments make your schedule tricky, and suggest a regular Zoom or FaceTime call to catch up. They’ll feel heard, and you’ll have a standing date instead of a standing guilt trip.

“Are you still not speaking to your brother/sister?”

What to say: “Whoa, that’s a lot to unpack over turkey. I’d rather enjoy the party. Have you tried the stuffing? It’s amazing.” Or the no-frills option: “That’s between the two of us, and I’d rather not get into that tonight.”

Why it works: The first option, says Gerber, kindly calls out that this isn’t the time and place, setting your boundary and redirecting the conversation right away. The blunter line points out that you avoid badmouthing anyone and that you don’t want advice or mediation from the peanut gallery. Adding “tonight,” Martinez notes, softens the message without opening the door. Pro tip: Always have food or drink on hand (literally) to pivot to. The stuffing never judges.

“How’s your divorce going?”

What to say:  “Thanks for asking. It’s a lot. I’d appreciate a break from thinking about it tonight. Tell me what you’ve been up to.”

Why it works: Many people who ask this one actually care, so Gerber’s answer is honest and reassures them while also making the topic off-limits for the evening. She thanks the other person for caring, states clearly that it’s not up for discussion and flips the conversation back to them. Either way, you don’t owe anyone a play-by-play of a hard time.

“How much money do you make?” or “When are you going to get a real job?”

What to say: “The pay’s fair, and I enjoy the work. Want to know what I enjoy most?” Or, for the “real job” jab: “This is my real job, and I really enjoy it. Want to know what I enjoy most?” For a laugh, you can also try: “Enough that I was able to buy that [item you wanted]!”

Why it works: You’re answering the spirit of the question without getting caught up in numbers. “By inviting curiosity, you’re turning judgment into a conversation,” Martinez says, “and your calm confidence doesn’t give much with which to argue.” 

If you’re between gigs or still figuring things out, Turinas also has a line for “So what are you doing with your life?” She suggests responding with: “Honestly, I’m figuring it out and enjoying the process.” It works, she says, because it “reframes uncertainty as a choice, not a failure.”

“Are you still renting? Don’t you think it’s time to buy a house?”

What to say: “Renting works for us right now. Have you seen the housing market?” Or: “Renting works for me. If anything breaks, I call the landlord; it’s their problem. Have you had anything break in your home recently?”

Why it works: Similar to the advice above about your career, the phrase “right now” frames renting as a choice, Martinez says, and pivots to a topic most people have opinions about.

The second version, says Gerber, is calm and confident and invites the asker to share their own homeowner woes. However, Gerber adds a warning about that one: There is always something to fix, so you may lose them to a 20-minute monologue about their gutters!

“Did you gain weight?”

What to say: “I’m not going to talk about my body, but I’d love to hear how you’ve been.” Or, to keep it lighter at first: “I’m feeling good, thanks.” And if they push: “I’m not interested in talking about my body. How was your trip?”

Why it works: According to Turinas, this is one question that deserves a firm boundary rather than a joke. “Comments about weight can be genuinely harmful,” she says. Nobody has to justify, explain or defend their body—period.

If you’re feeling spicy, Gerber suggests turning the tables: “Before I answer that, you go first. Tell me something deeply personal about yourself.” She says the asker usually realizes the mistake and apologizes. Lawton has another zero-frills option: “That is a very disrespectful question, and I do not appreciate it.”

A note for readers from Martinez: Skip comments on anyone’s body this season, including compliments on weight loss. “You never know who’s dealing with illness, grief or an eating disorder.”

“Are you pregnant?”

What to say: “Nope!” with a smile, and move on. If they persist: “If I have news like that, I’ll share when I’m ready.” Or, a lighter option: “No, just enjoying the holiday food.”

Why it works: A short, light answer ends the moment fast. And as Martinez points out, “You don’t have to rescue the asker from their embarrassment.” Gerber also likes the flip-back “Why do you ask?” here, delivered seriously, since it shows the person how personal the question really was.

Also, never ask this question yourself. As Martinez notes, the person in front of you could be in the middle of infertility treatments or coping with pregnancy loss.

“Why don’t you drink?”

What to say: “I just don’t, but I’d love a sparkling water!” Or, if you’d rather go with a laugh, Gerber suggests: “Trust me, if you’ve seen my dance moves, you know alcohol is unnecessary.”

Why it works: No reason is required, and people have many reasons to skip alcohol. Turinas says it plainly: “Giving reasons invites debate; a simple, upbeat answer ends it.” Martinez adds that keeping a drink in your hand, even a seltzer, cuts down on follow-ups.

For the minimalist, Lawton offers, “Not everyone drinks.”

“Who did you vote for?”

What to say: “I’d love to keep tonight politics-free. Tell me about your trip!” Or: “I’m taking the night off from politics, but I want to hear about your trip.”

Why it works: This sets a boundary on the topic, not on the person, Martinez says. And if you do want to engage, Turinas says that’s fine too, as long as you stay calm and avoid aggression: “I see it differently, and here’s why.” Either way, you get to choose, and staying calm keeps it a conversation instead of a fight. 

Bonus round!

Here are a few more quick hits from Martinez because yes, there are a lot of holiday minefields.

Question: “Is that what you’re wearing?”
Response: “Yep, I feel great in it!”

Question: “Are you still in therapy?”
Response: “I am, and I highly recommend it!”

Question: “Why didn’t you bring [partner/the kids]?”
Response: “They send their love. It worked out better this way this year.”

What else do you need to know about delivering these lines?

Mostly this: Tone does the work, and shorter is better. Here’s how to deliver your lines like a pro.

  • Practice out loud. It sounds silly, but it works. Rehearsing in the car, in the shower or to the dog is how a line goes from something you read to something that comes out of your mouth under pressure.
  • Decide your boundaries before you walk in. “Get clear on what you’re happy to talk about this year and what’s off the table,” Gerber says. You can even send a heads-up beforehand: “I’d love to just enjoy the day together, so I’m not getting into career talk this year.” Martinez adds that you can choose what’s open for discussion with whom. For example, you might tell your sister more than your uncle.
  • Pause before you answer. Gerber teaches a tool called the EQ Switch (her own term) that takes less than 10 seconds: “Pause, take a breath, notice what you’re feeling, and then choose your response instead of reacting.”
  • Keep your tone warm. As noted above, “tone does most of the work,” says Martinez. “The same words said with a smile sound gracious, and said sharply, they sound defensive.” Gerber’s trick is to shape your face like you’re saying the letter e, which makes you look approachable and friendly. Lawton prefers a calm, neutral expression, noting, “You can be nice and hold boundaries.”
  • Keep it short. “Short beats long. Overexplaining invites rebuttal,” Martinez says. The bottom line is that you don’t owe anyone a deep reason for your boundaries.
  • Redirect with a question about them. “Most people would rather talk about themselves anyway,” says Martinez. 
  • If they push, repeat once, then exit. “I really don’t want to get into that right now” works beautifully the second and third time too, says Gerber. When it stops working, give yourself an exit: “I think we’re circling back again. I’m going to grab a drink. I’ll be right back.” Stepping away to refill your plate or get some air is always allowed. 
  • Assume good intent. “Most people mean well,” Turinas says. “Assuming good intent helps you stay calm, even while you protect your boundaries.”
  • Recruit an ally. Martinez suggests asking someone you trust to step in when they see you cornered. Turinas says to agree on it in advance, so you can rescue each other. (Next time, my husband and I are working out a signal.)
  • Plan your recovery. If you tend to replay conversations afterward, build in a break during the event, like a walk, a call with a friend or some quiet time. “Be aware of your thoughts, but don’t treat them as proof that you handled things poorly,” Martinez says.
  • Expect imperfection. “Holidays are a mix of emotion, noise and awkwardness,” Gerber says. When you expect that, you feel less blindsided, and awkward moments, she adds, turn into “the best stories later.”

Which brings me back to my mumbled “We’re really excited about this.” It wasn’t the comeback of the century, but it was kind, it kept the party going, and, eventually, it turned into the opening of an article. Win/win! Awkward moments really do make the best stories. Mine just took a while to find its punch line.

About the experts

  • Sandy Gerber is a certified communication and emotional intelligence trainer, a TEDx speaker and the bestselling author of Emotional Magnetism, which has won more than 20 international book awards. She was named #16 on Global Gurus’ 2026 list of the World’s Top 30 Communication Professionals, received the 2025 Women of Influence Creative Innovator Award and hosts the Magnetic Communication podcast. Her upcoming book is Connected Conversations.
  • Igda Martinez, PsyD, is a licensed clinical psychologist at Ambit Psychological Services in New York, where she treats adults with anxiety, depression and trauma. 
  • Danyail Lawton is a strategic communications professional who served 23 years in the U.S. Air Force as an intelligence operations professional.
  • Emily Turinas, PhD, is a licensed psychologist in Austin, Texas, and the founder of Live Oak Psychology and Well Launched. She earned her PhD from the University of Texas at Austin and works with women navigating relationship patterns, family dynamics and life transitions.

articles.title: Here’s Why There Are 2 Spots to Latch Your Gas-Pump Nozzle (Hint: They Actually Do Different Things!)
articles.content:
Last year on a road trip, my wife and I were getting down to fumes and pulled in to a remote gas station. You know the type: two lonely pumps and an eerie sense of foreboding. After a couple of (hilarious) comments about soon being victims of a serial killer, she filled the tank, gripping the nozzle tightly and completely ignoring the little metal latch that dangled down.
Unless you’ve never left the state of New Jersey, where people aren’t allowed to pump their own gasoline (though diesel is OK), you’ve probably noticed that little latch while you’re filling up. But what’s it for, and why are there two or even three spots on the handle for you to stick that metal tab? The evolution follows our country’s broader automotive history, and it’s an interesting backstory, whether you use the latch or not.
I talked to Scott Boorse, the vice president of technical programs and industry affairs at the Petroleum Equipment Institute, to learn more about this ubiquitous, yet mysterious, little gas-nozzle latch. Read on to learn why these metal flaps are so useful and how they started popping up on gas pumps all over the country.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more interesting facts, news, tech, humor and travel all week long.
The latch, which Boorse says is actually called a “hold-open clip,” allows you to prop open the nozzle so fuel can be dispensed into your car’s tank without having to hold it open yourself. It’s integrated into the nozzle’s auto-shutoff function, so that when the tank reaches its maximum fill level, the pump stops. (More on this coming up.)
The clip can be seated in to two or three grooves that sit along the bottom of the nozzle handle. Why is there more than one choice? The different grooves allow people to control the speed of fuel delivery.
People like options. “When the clips first came out, there were three positions—let’s call them low, medium and high,” Boorse says. “Manufacturers would typically say that the lowest setting would be the minimum required to make the auto-shutoff function work properly, typically about 6 gallons per minute.”
But convenience-store owners wanted a faster setting so they could sell more gas. Boorse says when he worked for a high-volume retailer, they wanted a single hold-open-clip setting dispensing at roughly 8 gallons per minute. “We wanted people to get in as fast as they could, fill up all their fuel and leave, so we could get another customer in.”
So there are some marketing reasons behind the clip settings, Boorse says. That said, there’s only so much potential variation; 10 gallons per minute is about the maximum a dispenser can do. Today, it depends on the manufacturer and the end user’s requirements, though Boorse says many clips have moved to a two-position configuration. As for pumping gas slower? “Most people want things faster.”
No, and it’s been an interesting evolution, Boorse says. First came the auto-shutoff feature, which is a safety function built in to the fuel pump so that gas won’t spill out when the tank is full. Then came the hold-open clip, which was incorporated into the auto-shutoff in the 1950s; it was added as a convenience for full-service attendants.
“Initially, back in the days of full-service attendants, he or she would be doing other tasks,” like checking your oil and tire pressure or washing your windshield, Boorse says. But as we moved into an era of self-service, especially into the 1970s and ’80s, the hold-open clip became more of a customer convenience feature. That had some drawbacks.
“With the advent of a convenience-store model, what ended up happening is people would use the hold-open clip to pump their fuel, and then they would leave their vehicle and enter the store,” Boorse says. “That was kind of frowned upon by fire marshals.” So local jurisdictions often disallowed the clips, thinking customers would be forced to stay with their vehicles.
Not so much. “People started sticking all kinds of different things in there so they could go inside the store, use the bathroom or buy a cup of coffee, a newspaper or cigarettes,” Boorse says. One of the most common items people used were tennis balls, which did a great job of holding open the nozzle but were less successful at triggering the auto-shutoff. (Other popular hold-open-clip substitutes were Bic lighters, so let that one sink in.)
No surprise: Fires and spills at gas stations went up. “Fire marshals were like, ‘Now that I actually see this, it’s probably better to use the clip,'” Boorse says. Today, most jurisdictions realize the hold-open clip is part of the pump’s overall safety function, though he says there are still some “overzealous fire marshals” out there.
Convenience is the main one, but if you have arthritis or hand-strength limitations, the hold-open clip really comes in handy. Boorse says for a typical, 12-gallon gas tank, at 6 gallons a minute on the low setting, you’re looking at about two minutes to fill your entire tank. At full speed, you might cut that down to just over a minute.
That doesn’t sound like much, but if your grip strength is weak, holding open a gas nozzle, even for a minute or two, can feel like an eternity—or even be impossible.
No, and there’s no nationwide requirement to have them. Remember the local fire marshals Boorse mentioned? They’re the final word on the legality of hold-open clips within a certain jurisdiction, whether that’s a state, county, city, township or whatever. “You’ll still run into someone today who will be like, ‘We don’t allow the hold-open clip in our entire jurisdiction,'” Boorse says.
For this reason, manufacturers make gas nozzles with and without hold-open clips. “You can order the nozzle without it,” Boorse says. “Or it can also be removed. There are typically two rivets that hold the clip onto the nozzle.” (Of course, this would have to be done by an authorized service provider.)
As long as it’s working correctly, no. Boorse stresses that while the hold-open clip is a convenient way to pump gas, its main utility is safety. “The hold-open clip is one part of the overall safety features of the auto-shutoff function of the nozzle itself,” he says. Here’s how it works.
The gas nozzle has a check valve inside of it that allows fluid to flow in a single direction only. At the end of the nozzle (where it enters your car’s tank), there’s an opening that allows air to flow back toward the check valve, keeping it open. When the gas in the tank reaches the opening, it cuts off the air flow, creating a vacuum that closes the valve and stops the pump. The hold-open clip is designed to give way when this happens.
This doesn’t mean you can walk away when you use the clip, Boorse says. Getting back in your car can build up static electricity, which can spark a flash fire if you touch the nozzle without discharging the buildup. He also says once people get in their car, they tend to drive away with the nozzle still in the gas tank. “Believe it or not, that happens a lot more than you would think.”

Today, most jurisdictions realize the hold-open clip is part of the pump’s overall safety function, though he says there are still some “overzealous fire marshals” out there.

What are the other benefits to hands-free pumping?

Convenience is the main one, but if you have arthritis or hand-strength limitations, the hold-open clip really comes in handy. Boorse says for a typical, 12-gallon gas tank, at 6 gallons a minute on the low setting, you’re looking at about two minutes to fill your entire tank. At full speed, you might cut that down to just over a minute.

That doesn’t sound like much, but if your grip strength is weak, holding open a gas nozzle, even for a minute or two, can feel like an eternity—or even be impossible.

Do all pumps have hold-open clips?

No, and there’s no nationwide requirement to have them. Remember the local fire marshals Boorse mentioned? They’re the final word on the legality of hold-open clips within a certain jurisdiction, whether that’s a state, county, city, township or whatever. “You’ll still run into someone today who will be like, ‘We don’t allow the hold-open clip in our entire jurisdiction,'” Boorse says.

For this reason, manufacturers make gas nozzles with and without hold-open clips. “You can order the nozzle without it,” Boorse says. “Or it can also be removed. There are typically two rivets that hold the clip onto the nozzle.” (Of course, this would have to be done by an authorized service provider.)

Could the gas tank overflow while using the hold-open clip?

As long as it’s working correctly, no. Boorse stresses that while the hold-open clip is a convenient way to pump gas, its main utility is safety. “The hold-open clip is one part of the overall safety features of the auto-shutoff function of the nozzle itself,” he says. Here’s how it works.

The gas nozzle has a check valve inside of it that allows fluid to flow in a single direction only. At the end of the nozzle (where it enters your car’s tank), there’s an opening that allows air to flow back toward the check valve, keeping it open. When the gas in the tank reaches the opening, it cuts off the air flow, creating a vacuum that closes the valve and stops the pump. The hold-open clip is designed to give way when this happens.

This doesn’t mean you can walk away when you use the clip, Boorse says. Getting back in your car can build up static electricity, which can spark a flash fire if you touch the nozzle without discharging the buildup. He also says once people get in their car, they tend to drive away with the nozzle still in the gas tank. “Believe it or not, that happens a lot more than you would think.”

  • Jeff Prusko, lead standards project manager at UL Standards & Engagement; email interview, Nov. 13, 2026

articles.title: Hershey’s Is Selling Chocolate Bars for Just 5 Cents for One Day Only—Here’s How to Get Yours!
articles.content:
Hershey’s is taking chocolate lovers back to 1900 with a deal that’s almost impossible to believe in 2026. The company has announced that it’s bringing back the original five-cent price of its classic Milk Chocolate Bar, but it’s just for one day.
The special offer runs Wednesday, Nov. 25, to celebrate the theatrical release of HERSHEY, a new movie about chocolate pioneer Milton Hershey and his wife, Catherine “Kitty” Hershey. The film tells the story behind the couple’s rise and the chocolate business that became one of America’s most recognizable brands.
The five-cent bars will be available through select locations and retailers, but there are a few important details to know before heading out. Supplies are limited and purchase limits vary depending on where shoppers get their chocolate.
There are three ways to take advantage of the offer on Nov. 25, just before Thanksgiving, according to a news release from the company.
At Hershey’s Chocolate World in Hershey, Pennsylvania, the five-cent deal begins at 9 a.m. ET during regular operating hours. The Times Square location in New York City starts at 10 a.m. ET. Shoppers at both locations can purchase up to 10 classic bars per person, plus applicable tax.
But you don’t have to be at a Hershey store to grab this chocolate deal. Walmart is also participating, as is Amazon.
Starting at 9 a.m. ET, online shoppers can order a classic Hershey’s Milk Chocolate Bar for five cents through Walmart.com with a Walmart account (choose the pickup option). Those shopping in stores can purchase a bar and get cash back using the Ibotta app to upload a photo of their receipt. The limit is five bars per person, and the offer isn’t available for Ship to Home.
Amazon shoppers have another option. Starting at 9 a.m. ET, the five-cent bar will be available through Amazon Grocery with Same-Day Delivery in eligible areas. A promotional code shared on Hershey’s social media channels unlocks free shipping for qualifying addresses. The limit is two bars per person.
The deal applies to classic Hershey’s Milk Chocolate Bars, not the separate vintage-inspired packaging collection. All offers are available while supplies last.
